title: After My Hospital Clerkships at an Ivy League School and the Oldest Medical School in North America
paragraphs: I remember as if it were yesterday the day, March 25, 2016, when I left Chubu Centrair International Airport with my heart racing. Although it was a short two-month clerkship, I was fortunate to have the opportunity to go to the University of Pennsylvania in the United States to study pediatric pulmonology and medical oncology. It was made possible by benefiting from the tradition of the Nagoya University School of Medicine, and I cannot thank enough Dr. 粕谷, Dr. 長谷川 and 西尾-san of the International Collaboration Office, who supported me. It was my first time travelling to the United States, and I was a little anxious about entering the country, but I was able to enter without any problems together with my classmate 長井. In this report, I would like to summarise briefly, focusing on the two hospitals where I did clinical clerkships and on life in America.

Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania - Founded in 1765 as the first medical school in America, it puts great effort into both clinical care and research, and in any case its medical and research facilities were very well equipped. I heard that it receives more than 550 million dollars in research funding, the second largest in the country, and boasts the world's second-best record in the field of medical research, which I found convincing. I had some prior information from the internet, but seeing it in person I was overwhelmed by how remarkable it is. Its affiliated hospitals are the Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania (commonly HUP), the first university hospital in America, Pennsylvania Hospital (commonly Pennsy), the first hospital in America, and the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia (commonly CHOP), the first children's hospital in America, so Penn is truly the birthplace of American medicine. I was able to train at CHOP and Pennsy. I felt that the doctors, with the pride of an Ivy League school, are very enthusiastic about education.

Children's Hospital of Philadelphia (CHOP) - For the first month I rotated through pediatric pulmonology at CHOP. The building was larger than Nagoya University's (even finding rooms was a struggle and I often got lost in the first week), and because all departments are specialised in children, patients can receive ideal care, and they come from all over the world seeking cutting-edge pediatric care. The clerkship consisted of three kinds of work, consults, inpatient care and outpatient clinic, divided by week, and every day was truly stimulating and I was always using my brain. I was assigned to the consult team from the first day, and learned by accompanying the Attending, who was the Chief Director, and an excellent Fellow. On the first day I could barely keep up, but from the second day I asked questions actively and took part in discussions. For every patient I saw I was asked many questions, and was also asked my opinion about the treatment policy. Even so, I felt no wall at all between me and the senior doctors, I could say frankly what I thought, and it felt as if they worked enjoyably even when busy, with jokes and idle chat. Also, many people were interested in Japanese culture and medical care, and it was hard to explain. As for cases, there were many severe patients with cystic fibrosis (CF) and tracheomalacia, and there was a patient who went into cardiopulmonary arrest during bronchoscopy using a thin pediatric fiberscope, which was shocking. My impression of the outpatient clinic was that overall there were many CF and asthma patients. Besides bedside clerkship, I attended everything from respiratory physiology to the pediatric case conference for residents held every day at lunchtime (lunch is free, which is helpful for students), living the same life as the local medical students and residents and deepening interaction with them. I was also able to ask to observe the VEPTR surgery for scoliosis, invented by Dr. Campbell of CHOP. Through this clerkship I was able to reconfirm that if you clearly tell people what you are interested in and take the initiative yourself, many things become possible. "Where there is a will, there is a way."

Pennsylvania Hospital (Pennsy) - In the second month I trained in Hematology and Oncology, which I had long been interested in, at the oldest hospital in America with a long history. The hospital also has the oldest operating room in America, and for me, who aspires to be a surgeon, setting foot in such a historic place and touching the operating table was a very valuable experience. The clerkship was different from CHOP: basically we did consults and saw outpatients in the free time. I had thought I would just make rounds with the doctor and perhaps do a physical examination if given the chance, but when we received a consult, I did the interview and physical examination from the start without the doctor, summarised them on a consult sheet, later presented to the doctor, and then went to see the patient again. When I suddenly saw an AIDS patient in the psychiatric ward on the first day, I was very anxious, but 長井 was rotating at the same time, so the two of us cooperated and somehow got through. Gradually I became able to grasp the key points, and I think I gained ability over the month. I also learned about rare cancer cases and clinical trials, which was very educational. At the end, in the doctor's evaluation, I received Honors, the best grade, which gave me confidence and was a very good opportunity to think about what I want to do in the future. The distance from patients and medical staff is close, and to juniors who are considering Penn, I recommend a clerkship at Pennsy without hesitation.

Life in Philadelphia - During my stay I lived in a Penn dormitory called Sansom Place East. I could interact with people on the same floor and with my roommates, and I made many friends. The timing of the study abroad was also good, and everyone lay down on the deep green lawn to read books or chat with friends, and I too was able to have the campus life seen in movies. Philadelphia is a historic city with many tourist spots such as the Liberty Bell, but my favourite was the Philadelphia Museum of Art. It is a famous place that also appears in the Rocky film series, and when I had time I ran to the museum as training, and the live view from the top of the steps overlooking the city is beyond words. New York and D.C. are also near, about two hours by train or bus, so I could do sightseeing on weekends. I was also able to enter the clubhouse of Penn, the Ivy League school, in New York, which highlighted Americans' brand consciousness regarding universities. I have a mountain of other things I want to tell and cannot write them all, but every single thing I experienced in America was very valuable and will undoubtedly be nourishment for my future life, and it was two months I will never forget.
